facts.statehood_note: One of the original 13; Massachusetts became the sixth state to ratify the U.S. Constitution on February 6, 1788. Its official name is the Commonwealth of Massachusetts.
facts.motto: Ense petit placidam sub libertate quietem (Latin: By the sword we seek peace, but peace only under liberty)
facts.name_origin: Named for the Massachusett people. The name likely comes from a Wôpanâak (Wampanoag language) word often translated as 'near the great hill' or 'by the blue hills,' meaning the Blue Hills south of Boston.

government.chambers: Massachusetts Senate (40 members) and Massachusetts House of Representatives (160 members); members of both serve two-year terms
government.executive: Governor (4-year term), elected along with a lieutenant governor. The governor signs or vetoes laws, appoints judges, prepares the yearly budget, and commands the Massachusetts National Guard. An elected Governor's Council (the lieutenant governor plus eight councilors) reviews the governor's appointments and pardons.
government.courts: Supreme Judicial Court (a chief justice and six associate justices). All Massachusetts judges are appointed by the governor and confirmed by the Governor's Council.
government.local: 14 counties, but 8 county governments were abolished between 1997 and 2000. Most local government is done by 351 cities and towns (292 towns and 59 cities as of 2023), using the New England town system.
government.constitution: Constitution of the Commonwealth adopted in 1780 during the Revolutionary War and drafted by John Adams; it is the oldest functioning written constitution in continuous effect in the world.
government.kid_line: "All people are born free and equal and have certain natural, essential and unalienable rights." (Declaration of Rights, Article I, as rewritten by Amendment Article CVI; the 1780 original said "All men are born free and equal.")

long_ago.about: The Wampanoag, the 'People of the First Light,' have lived in what is now southeastern Massachusetts and eastern Rhode Island for more than 12,000 years. The Wampanoag Nation once included more than 67 tribal communities.
The Massachusett lived around Massachusetts Bay near the Blue Hills, and the state is named for them. Their leader Chickatawbut met Plymouth colonists in 1621 at a hill in today's Quincy.
The Nipmuc homelands stretch across central Massachusetts, northwestern Rhode Island, and northeastern Connecticut. Many Nipmuc people still live in Worcester County today.

The Pocumtuc lived where the Deerfield and Connecticut Rivers meet, in today's Franklin County. They grew corn, beans, and squash in the fertile meadows near Deerfield and fished in the Connecticut River.

today.about: A federally recognized tribe (re-acknowledged in 2007) with about 3,200 citizens and reservation land in Mashpee and Taunton.
A federally recognized Tribal Nation on the western end of Martha's Vineyard.
A state-recognized Nipmuc tribe; the Hassanamisco Nipmuc have had a formal relationship with the Commonwealth of Massachusetts since its Commission on Indian Affairs was created in 1976.
Received official state recognition by executive order of the governor in November 2024.

first_peoples.today_note: Massachusetts has two federally recognized tribes, the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe and the Wampanoag Tribe of Gay Head (Aquinnah). The Nipmuc Nation (Hassanamisco Nipmuc) and the Herring Pond Wampanoag have state recognition.
sites: Wampanoag Homesite at Plimoth Patuxet Museums, Plymouth, where Native people explain and demonstrate how Wampanoag ancestors lived
Moswetuset Hummock, Quincy, the hill where Massachusett leader Chickatawbut met Plymouth colonists in 1621

history.event: Wampanoag ancestors are living in what is now southeastern Massachusetts and eastern Rhode Island.
A disease brought by Europeans, most likely smallpox, kills about 90 percent of the Native people around Massachusetts Bay.
English Pilgrims sail on the Mayflower and start Plymouth Colony on Patuxet land; they sign the Mayflower Compact.
Puritans found the Massachusetts Bay Colony and Boston. The colony later banishes people who disagree with its leaders, such as Anne Hutchinson and Roger Williams.

King Philip's War: Wampanoag leader Metacom and allied Nipmuc, Pocumtuc, and Narragansett people fight English colonists who keep breaking agreements. Hundreds of Wampanoag people and their allies are executed or enslaved, and the Wampanoag lose most of their land.
The Battles of Lexington and Concord begin the American Revolutionary War.
Massachusetts adopts its constitution, drafted by John Adams, which says all men are 'born free and equal.'
Elizabeth Freeman, an enslaved woman, wins her freedom in court on August 22 by using the new constitution's words about equality.

Quock Walker, an enslaved man, leaves his enslaver Nathaniel Jennison in 1781, which starts a set of court cases. In 1783 Chief Justice William Cushing tells the jury that slavery cannot exist under the Massachusetts Constitution. It did not free every enslaved person at once, but it marked the end of slavery as a legal practice in Massachusetts.
On February 6, Massachusetts becomes the sixth state to ratify the U.S. Constitution.
Maine separates from Massachusetts and becomes the 23rd state.
Textile mills in Lowell and other cities make Massachusetts a leader of the Industrial Revolution, using water power and, later, immigrant workers.
The 54th Massachusetts Infantry, a regiment of Black soldiers, trains near Boston and attacks Fort Wagner, South Carolina, on July 18.
During Reconstruction, Lewis Hayden, who had escaped slavery, is elected to the Massachusetts legislature from Boston.

trailblazers.name: Elizabeth Freeman (Mum Bett)
trailblazers.text: Enslaved in Sheffield, she heard talk that all people are 'born free and equal' and went to a lawyer. In 1781 a jury set her free in Brom and Bett v. Ashley, and her case helped end slavery in Massachusetts. She chose the name Freeman and worked as a healer, midwife, and nurse.

trailblazers.name: Phillis Wheatley
trailblazers.text: Kidnapped from West Africa as a child and enslaved by the Wheatley family of Boston, she learned to read and write and became a poet. Her book Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773) made her the first African American to publish a book of poetry. She was freed soon after it came out.

trailblazers.name: Paul Cuffe
trailblazers.text: The son of a Wampanoag mother and an African father who had been enslaved, he became a sea captain, shipbuilder, and merchant. In Westport he founded a racially integrated school, and he spoke out against slavery.

trailblazers.name: Maria Mitchell
trailblazers.text: Born on Nantucket, she learned astronomy from her father. In 1847 she discovered a comet, known as 'Miss Mitchell's Comet,' and later became a professor of astronomy at Vassar College.

trailblazers.name: Lewis Hayden
trailblazers.text: He escaped slavery in Kentucky and settled in Boston. He and his wife Harriet Hayden sheltered many freedom seekers at their Beacon Hill home on the Underground Railroad, and in 1873 he was elected to the state legislature.

trailblazers.name: W. E. B. Du Bois
trailblazers.text: Born in Great Barrington, he became the first African American to earn a doctorate from Harvard. A writer and civil rights leader, he helped found the NAACP in 1909.

trailblazers.name: Jessie Little Doe Baird
trailblazers.text: A linguist who co-founded the Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project in Mashpee in 1993 to bring back the Wampanoag language, which had not been spoken for generations. Her work produced a Wampanoag-English dictionary of about 10,000 words, and she won a MacArthur Fellowship in 2010.

landforms: Taconic Range with Mount Greylock, the highest point
Islands of Martha's Vineyard and Nantucket
Glacial drumlins, kettle ponds, and moraines
geography.regions: From east to west: a coastal plain with Greater Boston and Cape Cod, the rocky hills of Central Massachusetts, the fertile Connecticut River Valley, and the Berkshire and Taconic mountains along the New York border.

ecosystems.name: Temperate deciduous forest
ecosystems.about: Forests cover about 62 percent of Massachusetts. Moose and black bears have returned to western forests as old farms grew back into woods.

ecosystems.name: Coastal beaches and islands
ecosystems.about: Beaches and small islands are breeding areas for roseate terns and the threatened piping plover, and Monomoy National Wildlife Refuge has a large population of gray seals.

ecosystems.name: Ocean waters
ecosystems.about: Offshore waters hold Atlantic cod, haddock, and American lobster, along with humpback whales and endangered North Atlantic right whales.

science.weather: Cold winters and warm summers. The coast is open to powerful nor'easters, tropical storms, and hurricanes; hurricane-force winds have hit the state 7 times since 1900. Heavy snowstorms, flooding, heat waves, and drought also happen.
science.resources: Massachusetts first depended on farming, fishing, and trade, then became a manufacturing center. Today its economy is led by higher education, biotechnology, technology, finance, health care, and tourism.
science.highlight: Dinosaur footprints near Mount Tom in the Connecticut River Valley come from the Mesozoic Era, when the valley formed as North America split from Europe and Africa.

g3_ss.title: Massachusetts Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Boston and the Bay State's coast on a map, meet cities and towns, and learn the jobs of the General Court, the governor, and the courts.

g3_ss.title: Massachusetts' First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Learn about the Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, and Pocumtuc long ago and today, including the Mashpee and Aquinnah Wampanoag.

g3_ss.title: Massachusetts Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Meet Elizabeth Freeman, Phillis Wheatley, Paul Cuffe, Maria Mitchell, and Jessie Little Doe Baird and tell how each made a difference.

g45_ss.title: Massachusetts' First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, and Pocumtuc homelands and ways of life, the 1617–1619 epidemic, and the language revival led by Jessie Little Doe Baird.

g45_ss.title: Plymouth, Massachusetts Bay, and King Philip's War
g45_ss.plan: Compare English colonies with Native nations' points of view, and examine King Philip's War and its results for the Wampanoag.

g45_ss.title: Massachusetts 1775–1877: Freedom and Reconstruction
g45_ss.plan: Trace the Revolution, the 1780 constitution and the freedom suits that ended slavery, Boston's Underground Railroad, the 54th Massachusetts, and Lewis Hayden's election in 1873.

g3_sci.title: Cape Cod Shores
g3_sci.plan: Explore beaches, piping plovers, terns, and gray seals and how sand shapes the cape.

g3_sci.title: Whales and the Gulf of Maine
g3_sci.plan: Meet humpback and right whales, cod, and lobster and learn why ocean animals need protection.

g3_sci.title: Nor'easters
g3_sci.plan: Learn what a nor'easter is, how snow and coastal flooding happen, and how families stay safe.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers Shaped Massachusetts
g45_sci.plan: Investigate how Ice Age glaciers left drumlins, kettle ponds, moraines, and Cape Cod itself.

g45_sci.title: Dinosaur Tracks of the Connecticut Valley
g45_sci.plan: Use the Mount Tom footprints to study fossils, rock layers, and how the valley formed.

g45_sci.title: Forests Come Back
g45_sci.plan: Study how farms turned back into forest and why moose and black bears returned, using data on forest cover.
